t: Count Numbers with Non-Decreasing Digits — Editorial
o:
We must count integers in [l, r] whose **base-b** representation has non-decreasing digits. The twist: l and r are given as *decimal* strings of up to 100 digits, so they cannot fit in any native integer type, and iterating the range is impossible.

**Example 1** (l="23", r="28", b=8): the values 23..28 in base 8 are 27, 30, 31, 32, 33, 34; only 27 (2≤7), 33 and 34 are non-decreasing → 3.

**Example 2** (l="2", r="7", b=2): binary forms 10, 11, 100, 101, 110, 111; only 11 and 111 qualify → 2.

Constraints imply: (1) all arithmetic on l, r must be done on digit strings (big-number subtraction by 1, and repeated division by b to convert decimal → base b, costing O(n²)); (2) once we have base-b digit arrays, the answer is a classic digit-DP / combinatorial count of f(r) − f(l−1).
k: Convert the decimal strings to base-b digit arrays using schoolbook repeated division by b — this works even for 100-digit numbers.
Answer = f(r) − f(l−1), where f(N) counts non-decreasing base-b strings ≤ N; allowing leading zeros makes every number have exactly one padded representation, so 0 needs no special casing.
Number of non-decreasing sequences of length m with digits in [v, b−1] is C(m + (b−1−v), m) (stars and bars), giving an O(n·b) closed-form count.

a.i: Build the base-b digits of N, then scan positions left to right tracking the previous digit p and whether we are still tight to N's prefix. From a free position, any non-decreasing completion works, so results depend only on (position, prev) — memoize those. Counting padded strings (leading zeros allowed) means every integer maps to exactly one digit string, and the string for 0 cancels out in f(r) − f(l−1).
s: Implement dec(s): subtract 1 from a decimal string with borrowing.
Implement toBase(s, b): repeatedly divide the decimal digit array by b, collecting remainders (LSB-first).
Define f(s): recursive go(i, p, tight) trying digits v from p to limit, recursing with tight' = tight && v == ds[i].
a.t: O(n² + n·b²) — the repeated-division base conversion is O(n²) total; the DP has O(n·b) memoized free states, each spending O(b) on transitions (tight path adds O(n·b)).
a.sp: O(n·b) for the memo table plus O(n) recursion depth and digit arrays.

a.i: Walk the base-b digits of N keeping the running minimum prev. At position i, choosing a digit v in [prev, ds[i]−1] makes the number strictly smaller than N regardless of what follows, and the remaining m positions can be filled with any non-decreasing sequence over [v, b−1], of which there are C(m + (b−1−v), m) by stars and bars. Summing these plus 1 for N itself gives f(N) directly — no memoization needed.
s: Precompute Pascal's triangle binomials up to n + b modulo 1e9+7.
Convert N to base-b digits (shared helpers dec/toBase as in Approach 1).
Scan digits left to right; for each position add C(m + (b−1−v), m) for every valid v < ds[i], updating prev.
If the whole prefix matched N (never broke), add 1 for N itself.
a.t: O(n² + n·b + (n+b)²) — base conversion dominates at O(n²); binomial table is O((n+b)²) and the scan is O(n·b).
a.sp: O((n+b)²) for the binomial table plus O(n) for digit arrays.

w:
**Which to pick:** In an interview, lead with the digit-DP framing (Approach 1) since it generalizes to many counting problems, then note the stars-and-bars closed form (Approach 2) as the optimal refinement — it removes the memo entirely and is easy to verify against the DP.

**Common pitfalls:**
- Forgetting that l and r are *decimal* strings while the property is about *base-b* digits — you must perform big-number base conversion, not parse into an integer type.
- Off-by-one on f(l−1): remember to decrement the decimal string with proper borrowing (e.g., "100" → "99") before converting.
- Mishandling the case where N's own digits are non-decreasing (add 1), and breaking out of the scan correctly when ds[i] < prev.
- Modulo negatives in C++/Java/JS: always normalize `(x % MOD + MOD) % MOD` after subtraction.

**Edge cases:** l == r; l = "1" (decrement gives "0", whose empty base-b representation contributes 1 and cancels); single-digit ranges; b larger than any digit of r.

**Follow-ups:** count numbers whose digits are strictly increasing/decreasing; handle b > 10 with arbitrary digit symbols; answer queries [l, r] online after preprocessing binomials once.
